o: Choose a non-empty subset maximizing the product of its elements. With n <= 13, brute force over 2^n subsets works, but a linear DP over (max product, min product) seen so far is cleaner: multiplying by a negative flips max/min, so track both extremes. Zeros are handled naturally (they can only produce 0, useful only when everything else is worse). Examples: [3,-1,-5,2,5,-9] → drop -1, take the rest → 1350; [-4,-5,-4] → best pair -4*-5=20.
k: Track both maximum and minimum products: a negative element swaps their roles.
Zeros and single negatives are covered by allowing 'skip' and initializing with the first element.
DP over elements with O(1) state beats 2^n enumeration.

a.i: For each element, new max = max(x, mx*x, mn*x) and new min = min(x, mx*x, mn*x); the 'x' term covers starting a fresh subset.
s: For each subsequent x, compute candidates {x, mx*x, mn*x}; update mx and mn.
a.t: O(n) — one pass with constant work

a.i: Enumerate all 2^n subsets (n <= 13), multiply elements, take the max. Simple and clearly correct.
s: For mask in 1..2^n - 1, compute the product of selected elements.
a.t: O(2^n · n) — all subsets with inner product computation

w: Prefer the DP; it generalizes to larger n. Pitfall: the subset must be non-empty — initializing with nums[0] and including the standalone-x candidate handles all-negative and single-element cases like [-9] → -9 and [0] → 0. Follow-up: maximum strength with exactly k students, needing a 2D DP over count.
